newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer says budget trend key EMU factor.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says budget trend key EMU factor.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Sunday he hoped Germany could meet the Maastricht Treaty deficit goal this year but said sustainable budgetary discipline was more important than hitting targets.
The central bank president also indicated that he was comfortable with current low inflation levels and saw no reason to change monetary policies.
"The three percent (budget deficit to GDP ratio set down in the Maastricht Treaty) is an important reference number -- there is no doubt of that," Tietmeyer told Germany's Hesse Radio.

"But more important than the one-off fulfilment, or bare undershooting or overshooting of this number, is the question as to whether countries' public finances ... are in a condition that can be viewed as sustainable, and lastingly sustainable."

Tietmeyer said a convincing reform of the German tax system was essential to get the economy in shape. He said he saw no reason for the German central bank to deviate from its steady hand policy on interest rates.
"Steady hand monetary policy is something that I believe has paid off, which is correct, which is necessary. And at the moment I see no reason to change this monetary policy," he said.

In the run-up to a single currency the deficit target is one of several criteria in the Maastricht Treaty that prospective participants in economic and monetary union (EMU) must meet in 1997 to adopt the euro when it is launched in 1999.

But key European Union members are having difficulty meeting the targets. France last week said its deficit would probably exceed three percent this year and Germany is still struggling to meet the target.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel recently locked horns with the Bundesbank over a plan to revalue the central bank's currency and gold reserves to use the additional profits to rein in budget deficits ahead of monetary union.

But Tietmeyer said revaluing gold lodged at the Bundesbank would not under current rules yield any payout to Bonn. He also stressed that while the sale of gold reserves would in theory generate a payout, this was not an option for the German central bank and there was no pressure from Bonn to do so.

Asked how Waigel could benefit from Bundesbank gold reserves, Tietmeyer said: "According to the rules applying, this would only work if gold reserves were to be sold. But the government has made clear that it will not in any way force the Bundesbank to sell gold. To that extent it is not an issue."

The Bundesbank and Bonn have agreed to revalue currency reserves, largely dollars, but with the stipulation that any extraordinary payout does not occur this year, the crucial year for the choice of participants in monetary union.

Commenting on the recently-elected French Socialist-led government, Tietmeyer said French monetary policy was running on a stable course and that he saw no risk to the franc-deutschemark exchange rate from the new government.
"I believe that French monetary policy is on a very stable course and I assume that the franc-mark relationship is not up for discussion," Tietmeyer said.

Noting that the franc-mark relation had been relatively stable of late, Tietmeyer said: "If I have understood the politics correctly, the new government will do what it can not to put this result at risk."

He denied that the Bundesbank had declared patronage for the franc in the past, by which he meant it had made no agreement with the Bank of France under which the Bundesbank would offer its help should the franc come under pressure.
But he said it had helped the franc to win market trust in the past.
"And I see no reason why this should not also be so in the future. Declarations of patronage are not necessary," he said.

Tietmeyer noted that the job creation schemes being mooted in France ran counter to previous policies but said such policies were still at an early stage and had not translated into concrete budget strategies.
"We must wait and see. But I am convinced that people in France see very clearly how important a stable exchange rate between the French franc and the other European currencies is."
-- Frankfurt Newsroom, 49 69 7565 25
